name: style-conversational
title: Conversational: warm, spoken register for consumer software
description: A warm, spoken register: the voice the Mailchimp Content Style Guide describes and is itself written in, the plain-language guidance behind it, and the long-form house style of 37signals. The register is defined more by what it asks for than by what it rules out, so seven of these eight bands are floors, with the register’s own maximum recorded in each `measured` field and no edge on the far side. That is a real limitation and not a design: a document can run further into the permitted direction than any document in either corpus and this profile stays quiet. Only the rhythm band is two-sided. Every edge was measured over a 19-document reference corpus in the target register and contrasted with 12 documents of local technical prose in another register. The numbers are one reading of one corpus and they are the first thing to change: a finding that keeps coming back is sometimes a reason to move the band rather than the document.

corpus.note: Reference corpus in the target register, fetched 2026-08-28: 17 chapters of the Mailchimp Content Style Guide (github.com/mailchimp/content-style-guide, master), 3 Mailchimp help-centre articles, the 37signals Guide to Internal Communication, two Shape Up chapters and the Getting Real front matter. 19 of those documents clear the gate described below, for 24,363 words. A contrasting corpus of 12 documents / 15,120 words of local human technical prose was measured the same way and appears in every `measured` field as the off-register comparison. Edges sit just outside the reference range rather than at p10/p90, which makes them deliberately conservative and under-report rather than misdescribe good register prose. Prose gate: 35 words a sentence, the engine default 4 on the short side. Derived rather than chosen. Sorted by words per sentence, the reference corpus runs 8.3 to 22.9 and then jumps to 39.9 and 78.8; the local corpus runs 13.3 to 30.3 and then jumps to 38.0, 43.5, 57.9, 57.9, 79.5 and 135.8. Every document above those jumps that was read turned out to be headings, a table, navigation chrome or a bulleted file listing that the extractor had flattened into one long pseudo-sentence, so 35 sits in the empty band between the prose and the markup in both corpora and keeps 19 of 21 reference documents. An earlier draft of this profile ran the gate at 200 words a sentence, which admitted two of those flattened documents. One of them, the Getting Real front matter, is a duplicated list of chapter titles carrying no sentences at all, and it alone was holding the reference minimum for sentence endings down at 12.7 per 1000 (25.1 without it) and the reference minimum for first-person pronouns down at 0.0 (4.3 without it). Two of this set’s stated calibration anchors were therefore artefacts of one table of contents. Both are corrected here and every band below is re-derived at the narrower gate.

voice: Second person, and a speaker who says “we”. Contractions wherever they sound natural. Short sentences with the occasional long one, and a very short one after it. A question now and then, answered in the next line. Verbs doing the work instead of nouns built out of verbs. Read it out loud: if it is not something one person would say to another across a table, it is not this register.

notMechanised.name: sentence-length-long
notMechanised.note: Shipped in version 0.1.0 at 30 sentence endings per 1000 words and withdrawn here, on arithmetic rather than taste. The rule and the prose gate measure the same quantity: a rate of endings at or below E per 1000 words is exactly an average sentence of 1000/E words or longer, and the gate admits a document only up to `maxSentenceWords`. At the 30 edge the rule needed 33.3 words a sentence or more; the gate that the two corpora actually support is 35. The firing window is therefore 33.3 to 35 words a sentence, which is a coincidence and not a band. Loosening the gate to make room is what the 0.1.0 draft did, and the result was that every one of the eight documents it reported across 39 measured documents — six local, two reference — was a table, a bulleted listing or a page of navigation chrome rather than a document of long sentences. Zero of eight described what the rule names. The constraint it needs is a way to separate a missing full stop from a long sentence, and the engine has no such knob. The extreme is still covered from outside: `economist/long-sentences` reports at 20 endings per 1000 with its own gate at 120.

notMechanised.name: sentence-length-short
notMechanised.note: A ceiling on very short sentences. Self-contradictory here. The reference corpus reaches 120 endings per 1000 words, about 8 words a sentence, in prose the guide holds up as a model, so any non-vacuous ceiling would report the register’s own writing. This register has no sentence it considers too short.

notMechanised.name: initial-conjunction
notMechanised.note: A floor on sentence-initial And/But/So, sourced from Mailchimp’s “Write like a human.” Measured and declined: reference min 0.00, p10 0.00, median 0.00, maximum 8.10, with 10 of the 19 reference documents at zero. More than half the target corpus never opens a sentence that way, so a floor at 0 would report more than half of the register’s own writing. That is noise rather than a band.

notMechanised.name: semicolon-paren
notMechanised.note: Mailchimp is plain that semicolons “usually support long, complicated sentences that could easily be simplified”, and the metric separates the two corpora enormously. Declined because the shared vocabulary bundles “;” with “()” while the guide uses parentheses freely, so the local corpus’s large rate is mostly parentheses inside technical prose. It would measure markup habits rather than register.

notMechanised.name: em-dash
notMechanised.note: Investigated in both directions and declined on the source. The Mailchimp guide prescribes the em dash: “Use an em dash (—) without spaces on either side to offset an aside”, and recommends one in place of a semicolon. A band in either direction would contradict the guide this profile cites. Recorded as a `tension` entry against rules/em-dash instead.

notMechanised.name: comma
notMechanised.note: Measured, no discrimination worth a band. Reference 25.89 (min) / 42.36 (median) / 77.50 (max) against local 23.68 / 56.25 / 79.14: the ranges sit almost on top of each other and any edge outside one corpus is outside the other.

notMechanised.name: hedging
notMechanised.note: Named in the sources and real in them, but there is no hedge metric in the shared vocabulary and the honest expression of it is a span regex, which a style profile does not use. It belongs in an ordinary rule set rather than here.

notMechanised.name: unmeasurable guidance
notMechanised.note: Guidance read in the primary sources that has no rate over a document and so was not turned into one: “Use positive language rather than negative language”; “Be specific. Cut the fluff”; “Write in plain English”; “Our humor is dry … we prefer winking to shouting”; “Use exclamation points sparingly”; “Lead with the main point”; “When in doubt, read your writing out loud”; and Basecamp’s “Writing solidifies, chat dissolves”. None has a defensible counter-example, so none was made into a rule.

tension.note: The largest conflict in the set by a wide margin, and the one to read first. It reports consecutive sentences sharing a word skeleton, and parallel construction is how this register teaches: “Use sentence case for checkboxes and radio buttons. Use title case for drop-down menu names.” “We weren’t going to allow dragging events between days. We weren’t going to span multiple days.” Across the 19 reference documents it accounts for 47 of the 101 findings that are not em dashes when every rule set in this repo is loaded, and 49 of 76 when only the three sets this repo’s own slop.json selects are. Largest either way. Both readings of such a passage are accurate; which one applies is a judgement about the passage, and this profile does not make it for you. If you want the finding quiet for a document in this register, that belongs in the ignore list of your own slop.json, in your repo, under your name.

This repo’s own slop.json selects the em-dash set, which reports every em dash: 33 across the reference corpus. The Mailchimp guide asks for a true em dash to offset an aside and recommends one in place of a semicolon, so a document in this register carries some. That is why this profile ships no em-dash band in either direction: the reference corpus ran 0.00 (min) / 0.49 (median) / 4.05 (max) per 1000 words, far under any threshold worth setting, and what to do about the finding belongs in your own config.

The head-on one. The simonwillison set reports two or more questions in a row; 9 findings across the reference corpus, including a run of nine in the 37signals guide. This profile’s question-low rule requires questions, so the two point in opposite directions on the same passage by construction. The Federal Plain Language Guidelines go further than Mailchimp and recommend question headings outright. Both verdicts are separately labelled and both are correct about what they describe.

The sharpest small one. The slop-gate candidate reports “feel free to”, and it fires 3 times across the reference corpus. One of those is in the Mailchimp TL;DR chapter, on the sentence “Feel free to use contractions” — which is the sentence this profile’s contraction band cites as its source. The guide and the rule disagree about the same four words, and the disagreement is observed rather than hypothetical.

Three consecutive sentences opening on the same word: 6 findings across the reference corpus, all of them lists of parallel instructions in the Mailchimp guide. A deliberate device in spoken prose and a common one in this register. The finding describes the shape correctly either way.

The economist candidate set reports documents with no parentheses at all: 5 findings across the reference corpus against 1 across the local one, which makes it one of the few rules that leans against this register specifically rather than against technical prose. Short spoken sentences put the aside in a comma or an em dash instead of a bracket, which is what the Mailchimp guide asks for. It also fires on both of this profile’s own in-register examples.

4 findings across the reference corpus, on constructions such as “note how specific the idea is”. Listed for completeness rather than as a real opposition: nothing in this profile asks for the construction, and the overlap is with the register’s plain-spoken syntax rather than with any band here.

3 findings across the reference corpus, including “empowering” in the Mailchimp voice-and-tone chapter. Consumer-software writing uses the vocabulary that rule catalogues because it is that industry’s own vocabulary, which is a hazard of the subject rather than of the register. Same for ai-vocab, 3 findings, and colon-triple, 3.

Reported alongside not-because-because and whole because all three land on this profile’s own picture of the register rather than on any corpus. The two in-register examples carried by the rules below contain “If you wouldn’t say it, don’t send it”, “Not because plain is clever. Because plain is easy to read” and “That’s the whole trick”, and a slop rule reports each of them. Together the two examples draw 7 findings across 1,426 words, which is 4.91 per 1000 and above the 3.0 this repo sets for its own documentation. A profile whose model of good prose reads that way is not evidence that either side is mistaken, but it is the clearest single illustration of why these two kinds of rule set are kept apart and read separately.

Listed to head off a misreading of the raw counts. It produces 9 findings on the reference corpus, which puts it near the top of the table, but 17 on the local corpus — 1.12 per 1000 words there against 0.37 here. It leans harder against off-register technical prose than against this register, so despite the count it is not a conflict with this profile at all.

A question whose next sentence answers it. Question-and-answer is the shape this register’s educational content is built from, so the opposition is real in principle — but it produced 0 findings across the 19 reference documents, so unlike the entries above this one is reasoned rather than observed, and it is listed on that footing.

Carried as a conflict in version 0.1.0 on the strength of a reference document said to run at 4.0 commas per 1000 words, and withdrawn here. That document was the Getting Real front matter, a list of chapter titles admitted by a prose gate that was too wide. Measured at the corrected gate the reference corpus runs 25.89 (min) / 42.36 (median) / 77.50 (max), so no document in the target register comes near the economist edge of 20 and the conflict is not observed. Kept in this list only so the retraction sits beside the claim.

The humanizer-de set puts its rhythm edge at cv 0.4 and this profile puts its own low edge at 0.45. At or below 0.4 both report and say compatible things; between 0.40 and 0.45 only this profile does. Composition rather than conflict, but the two numbers sit close enough together to be worth stating, and 0.40 is also the number this profile would have to adopt to clear its own reference corpus, which is the reason its rhythm rule is labelled provisional below.

The entries above invite a tidy conclusion that the measurement does not support, so here is the whole of it. Counting findings per 1000 words over documents that clear this profile’s gate, em dashes excluded: with only the three sets this repo’s slop.json selects, the target-register reference corpus draws 3.12 and the off-register local corpus 1.65, a lean of about 1.9 to 1 against the register this profile asks for. Load every candidate set as well and the two converge to 4.15 and 3.90, which is no separation at all, because the wider pool picks up as much on technical prose as on spoken prose. So whether this register is slop-adjacent depends on which sets you have loaded, and any single ratio quoted without that qualifier is a number without a meaning. Two further cautions. Across the 31 gated documents of both corpora the correlation between second-person rate and non-em-dash finding rate is r = 0.10, which is nothing: an individual document does not draw more comment by moving further into the register. And these counts are of findings, not of agreement — no attempt was made here to judge how many of them a careful reader would sustain.

rules.name: Fewer contractions than this register uses
rules.description: Contracted forms — it’s, you’re, don’t, that’s — counted per 1000 words. This register runs 10 to 65 per 1000 across the reference corpus, with a median of 19, and it has no upper edge: no quantity of contraction reads as too spoken here, and none is recorded above which one would. At or below 6 the document is written out in full forms throughout, which lands nearer a memo than a conversation. It is a measurement of fit, not a defect: plenty of good writing sits outside it.
rules.suggest: Contractions are scarcer here than the conversational band expects, which is 6 or more per 1000 words. If you want this register, let the spoken forms stand where they already sound natural read aloud. If you do not, the band is the thing to change.
rules.measured: floor 6/1000. Reference corpus, 19 documents / 24,363 words in the target register: 9.71 (min) / 10.38 (p10) / 18.80 (median) / 38.01 (p90) / 64.77 (max). The floor sits 38% below the reference minimum rather than at p10, and 0 of 19 reference documents cross it. Local corpus, 12 documents / 15,120 words of human technical prose: 0.00 / 6.35 (median) / 27.27 (max), and 6 of 12 cross it. The far side is unmeasured: no ceiling is shipped, so a document may run above 65 per 1000 and this rule stays quiet.
rules.note: Sourced: “Feel free to use contractions” (Mailchimp Content Style Guide, TL;DR) and “They’re great! They give your writing an informal, friendly tone” (Grammar and Mechanics). The Federal Plain Language Guidelines put the same point as “‘Write as you talk’ is a common rule of writing readably, and the best way to do that is to use contractions.” The pattern also counts possessive ’s, which lifts the rate for documents full of names; both corpora carry the same lift, so the two are comparable. Prose gate: 35 words a sentence, the engine default 4 on the short side. Derived rather than chosen. Sorted by words per sentence, the reference corpus runs 8.3 to 22.9 and then jumps to 39.9 and 78.8; the local corpus runs 13.3 to 30.3 and then jumps to 38.0, 43.5, 57.9, 57.9, 79.5 and 135.8. Every document above those jumps that was read turned out to be headings, a table, navigation chrome or a bulleted file listing that the extractor had flattened into one long pseudo-sentence, so 35 sits in the empty band between the prose and the markup in both corpora and keeps 19 of 21 reference documents. The formal technical document in tests.hit is prose, not a config dump: it is genuinely below this register’s floor, which is the rule working rather than failing. It only sat in tests.miss while the prose gate was excluding it for having long sentences.

miss: Let's talk about your first send. You've built the list, you've picked a template, and now you're staring at a blank subject line, wondering what on earth goes in it. What do you actually write? Start with the thing you'd say to a friend across a table, in the ordinary words you would use if that friend had asked you the question out loud. If you wouldn't say it, don't send it. That's the whole trick. It takes a minute to learn and about a year to trust, and we still catch ourselves reaching for the fancy version when we are tired or in a hurry or trying to sound like a bigger company than we are. The plain one wins almost every time. Not because plain is clever. Because plain is easy to read on a phone, at a bus stop, with one thumb and half your attention. So write the subject line, then cut it in half, and read what is left out loud. Does it sound like you? Good. Send yourself a test. Look at it on your phone rather than your laptop, since that is where most of your readers are going to meet it, and check the little grey preview line next to the subject, which almost everybody forgets until an email goes out with a stray note about viewing it in a browser. Write something there. Anything beats that. Then hit send and go for a walk, because the numbers will still be there in an hour and they will look kinder after coffee. If the open rate disappoints you, change one thing next week. One. Change the subject line, or the send time, or the first sentence, and hold the rest steady, so that you learn something real instead of guessing in the dark. That is how we do it, and it is how our steadiest customers do it too. You will get quicker at this. Give it three sends before you judge yourself, and if you get stuck, ask us, because we would much rather answer a question than watch you stall.

So you've got a list, a template, and about forty minutes before the meeting. Let's use them well. The first thing to know is that nobody is going to read your email the way you're about to read it, sitting still, at a desk, with the whole thing in front of them. They'll see it on a phone, in a queue, with one thumb. That changes what matters. It means the subject line is doing most of the work, the first sentence is doing the rest, and everything after that is for the people you've already convinced.
What goes in the subject line? Say the thing. If the sale ends Friday, the subject line is that the sale ends Friday. We know that sounds obvious, and we know it isn't what most people do, because most people reach for the clever version first. We do it too. Then we read it out loud and put it back.
Here's a test that costs nothing. Write your subject line, then imagine saying it to someone across a table. If you'd feel silly saying it, you'll feel worse when twenty thousand people read it. Cut it in half and try again. You'll usually find the second half was the part you actually meant.
Now the preview text, which is the little grey line your reader sees next to the subject. Most people leave it empty, and their reader gets a stray note about viewing the message in a browser instead. Don't do that to yourself. Write one short line that adds something the subject didn't say. It's the cheapest win in the whole email and it takes about eight seconds.
The body is where people overthink it. You don't need an opening paragraph that clears its throat. Start with the thing. If your reader stopped after the first sentence, would they still know what you wanted? If not, move the point up. Everything else can wait, and most of it can go.
Keep your paragraphs short. Two or three sentences is plenty on a phone. Give the eye somewhere to rest. If you have a list of things, make it a list, because a list on a screen is easier than a sentence with four commas in it. And if you're explaining a process, number the steps, so your reader can find their place again after the interruption that is definitely coming.
One link, or two at most. We know it's tempting to add the blog post, the help article, the case study and the thing your colleague asked you to include. Every extra link splits your reader's attention, and attention doesn't divide neatly. Pick the one you'd keep if you could only keep one. Put the others in next week's email, which now has something to be about.
What about images? Use them when they say something words can't. A photograph of the thing you're selling earns its place. A stock picture of people shaking hands does not, and it costs your reader a second of loading on a train. Give every image alternative text, because a good number of your readers will never see it, and because their mail client may not load it either.
Then test. Send it to yourself, and read it on your phone before you read it anywhere else. Read it out loud while you're at it, which sounds ridiculous until the first time it saves you. You'll hear the sentence that doesn't work. You always do.
When it's ready, send it, and then go and do something else. The numbers will still be there in an hour, and they'll look kinder after a walk. Refreshing a dashboard on send day has never taught anyone anything, and we say that as people who have done it more often than we'd like to admit.
A week later, look properly. What do you want to know? Probably whether more people opened it than last time, and whether the ones who opened it did the thing you asked. Those are two different questions and they have two different answers. A great subject line with a weak offer gets you a good open rate and nothing else. A quiet subject line with a strong offer can beat it on the number that pays the bills.
So change one thing. One. Change the subject line, or the send time, or the first sentence, and hold everything else steady. If you change three things and the numbers move, you've learned that something worked, which is not the same as learning what. Give it three sends before you draw any conclusion at all, because a single send tells you about a single Tuesday.
And keep a note. Not a spreadsheet, unless you like spreadsheets. A short list of what you changed and what happened is enough, and it's worth more in six months than any report you could generate. Your memory of what worked in March will be confident and wrong. The note won't be.
That's most of it. There's a lot more you could learn, and none of it matters as much as sending the next one. If you're stuck, ask us. We would much rather answer a question now than read a post-mortem later, and we've yet to meet the question that was too small to send.
One more thing, and then we'll let you get on with it. The best email we sent last year was four sentences long and took a colleague of ours about six minutes to write. It went out on a Wednesday afternoon with a subject line that said exactly what was in it, no picture, one link, and a sign-off that sounded like a person. We have spent whole weeks on emails that did a tenth as well. Nobody on our team enjoys admitting that, and all of us have stopped arguing with it.
So when you find yourself on the fourth draft, ask whether the fourth draft is better or merely different. If you can't tell, it's different. Send the second one. Your reader has never seen any of the drafts and doesn't care how long it took you, and the only version that has ever helped anybody is the one that actually goes out.
Good luck with the send. Tell us how it goes, and if it goes badly, tell us that too, because those are the messages we learn the most from and the ones we get least often.

rules.name: The reader is addressed less than this register expects
rules.description: Second-person pronouns — you, your, yours — per 1000 words. This register runs 8 to 53 per 1000 with a reference median of 21, and there is no upper edge: it has no quantity of “you” it objects to, and none is recorded. At or below 6 the document describes a system rather than speaking to a person. It is a measurement of fit, not a defect: reference and analytic prose are doing a different job.
rules.suggest: The reader is addressed less often here than the conversational band expects, which is 6 or more second-person pronouns per 1000 words. If you want this register, address the reader directly and let each sentence say who does what. If you do not, the band is the thing to change: analytic and reference prose sits here legitimately, and this may simply be the wrong profile for the document.

So you've got a list, a template, and about forty minutes before the meeting. Let's use them well. The first thing to know is that nobody is going to read your email the way you're about to read it, sitting still, at a desk, with the whole thing in front of them. They'll see it on a phone, in a queue, with one thumb. That changes what matters. It means the subject line is doing most of the work, the first sentence is doing the rest, and everything after that is for the people you've already convinced.
What goes in the subject line? Say the thing. If the sale ends Friday, the subject line is that the sale ends Friday. We know that sounds obvious, and we know it isn't what most people do, because most people reach for the clever version first. We do it too. Then we read it out loud and put it back.
Here's a test that costs nothing. Write your subject line, then imagine saying it to someone across a table. If you'd feel silly saying it, you'll feel worse when twenty thousand people read it. Cut it in half and try again. You'll usually find the second half was the part you actually meant.

Most people leave it empty, and their reader gets a stray note about viewing the message in a browser instead. Don't do that to yourself. The body is where people overthink it. You don't need an opening paragraph that clears its throat. Start with the thing. If your reader stopped after the first sentence, would they still know what you wanted? If not, move the point up. Everything else can wait, and most of it can go.

rules.measured: floor 2/1000. Local corpus, 12 documents / 15,120 words of human technical prose: 0.00 / 0.00 (median) / 24.83 (max), and 7 of 12 cross it. Version 0.1.0 of this rule reported that one reference document sat at zero and that roughly 5% of the register’s own prose fell below the floor; that document was the Getting Real front matter, a list of chapter titles admitted by a prose gate that was too wide, and the claim does not survive the narrower gate. The far side is unmeasured: no ceiling is shipped.
rules.note: Sourced: “Refer to Mailchimp as ‘we,’ not ‘it’” (Mailchimp Content Style Guide, Grammar and Mechanics) and “Using ‘we’ to refer to your agency makes your agency more approachable” (Federal Plain Language Guidelines). Both corpora were measured with the same pattern, so the band is internally consistent, but a document that opens most sentences with “We” reads lower here than it deserves. The in-register example below is a case in point: it is full of “We know” and “We have” and still measures only 13 per 1000. Prose gate: 35 words a sentence, the engine default 4 on the short side. Derived rather than chosen. rules.name: Fewer questions than this register puts to the reader
rules.description: Question marks per 1000 words, over documents of 1000 words or more. This register runs 0 to 12 per 1000 with a reference median of 3.3, and there is no upper edge: a run of questions is one of the things it does on purpose. At exactly zero, across a thousand words or more, the document never turns to the reader and never uses the question-and-answer shape this register builds explanations from. It is a measurement of fit, not a defect: a shorter piece that happens to ask nothing is ordinary here, which is why this rule does not look at one.
rules.suggest: Nothing is put to the reader as a question, and the conversational band expects at least one across a document this long. If you want this register, a question heading, or a question the next paragraph answers, is the usual way in. If you do not, the band is the thing to change.
rules.measured: floor 0/1000, the most conservative floor the metric allows, over documents of 1000 words or more. Reference corpus, 19 documents / 24,363 words in the target register: 0.00 (min) / 0.00 (p10) / 3.29 (median) / 10.60 (p90) / 11.92 (max). The length threshold is the whole of this rule’s calibration and it was measured rather than chosen. At the set’s usual 250-word threshold this rule reports 4 of 19 reference documents — 21% of the register’s own prose — because a short help article that asks nothing is unremarkable here; all four sit between 597 and 840 words. Every one of the 9 reference documents at or above 1000 words asks at least one question, so the threshold takes the reference crossing rate from 4/19 to 0/9 while leaving the separation intact: 3 of the 5 local documents at or above 1000 words still cross. The far side is unmeasured: no ceiling is shipped, and a document may run above 12 per 1000 with nothing said here.
rules.note: Weakest rule in the set: params.max is 0, so it fires only on prose containing literally no question at all. Conversational writing asks questions far more often than never, but no corpus measurement was available to set a real floor, so the threshold stays where it cannot produce a false positive. Raise it once you have measured your own reference corpus.

rules.name: Sentence lengths outside the range this register moves in
rules.description: Sentence-length variation, as the coefficient of variation: standard deviation over mean. The one two-sided band in this set, and the only one whose permitted direction is bounded. This register runs 0.41 to 1.76 with a reference median of 0.71. At or below 0.45 the sentences are close to a single length: correct, readable prose that does not move the way speech moves. At or above 1.85 the length swings further than anything measured in the register, which reads as lurching rather than spoken. It is a measurement of fit, not a defect.
rules.suggest: Sentence lengths sit outside the range this register moves in, which is a variation between 0.45 and 1.85. Below it, let one sentence run long and the next one land short; above it, the swings are wider than speech makes. If you want neither, the band is the thing to change.
rules.measured: band cv 0.45 to 1.85, and the least evidenced band in the set on both edges. Reference corpus, 19 documents / 24,363 words in the target register: 0.41 (min) / 0.48 (p10) / 0.71 (median) / 1.39 (p90) / 1.76 (max). Local corpus, 12 documents / 15,120 words of human technical prose: 0.49 (min) / 0.75 (median) / 1.54 (max). The low edge at 0.45 sits between the reference minimum and p10 and reports 2 of 19 reference documents, which is 11% of the register’s own prose and the only band here that does so; the value that would clear the reference corpus is 0.40, and 0.40 is exactly humanizer-de/uniform-sentence-length, so at that setting this rule would be a duplicate of a rule that already exists. It is shipped at 0.45 knowing both of those things. The high edge at 1.85 sits 5% above the reference maximum, is crossed by 0 of the 31 measured documents, and is proven live only by the example below.
rules.note: The least directly sourced rule in the set, labelled as such on purpose, and the first to retune or drop. Neither guide states anything about sentence-length variation; the nearest thing is Mailchimp’s “When in doubt, read your writing out loud”, and speech is neither metronomic nor arbitrary. The numbers came from measuring the reference corpus; the reasoning behind wanting numbers at all did not. Version 0.1.0 shipped only the low edge; the high edge is added here so the rule describes a band rather than a floor, but it is an edge drawn just outside the observed range and no source asks for it. Prose gate: 35 words a sentence, the engine default 4 on the short side. Derived rather than chosen. Sorted by words per sentence, the reference corpus runs 8.3 to 22.9 and then jumps to 39.9 and 78.8; the local corpus runs 13.3 to 30.3 and then jumps to 38.0, 43.5, 57.9, 57.9, 79.5 and 135.8. Every document above those jumps that was read turned out to be headings, a table, navigation chrome or a bulleted file listing that the extractor had flattened into one long pseudo-sentence, so 35 sits in the empty band between the prose and the markup in both corpora and keeps 19 of 21 reference documents.
